title: BFS: Introduction
summary: Level-by-level tree/graph traversal using a queue; guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.

sections.heading: What is BFS?
sections.body:
**Breadth-First Search (BFS)** is a level-by-level traversal algorithm for trees and graphs.

Unlike DFS which dives deep into one path before backtracking, BFS explores **all nodes at the current level** before moving to the next level.

BFS uses a **queue** to ensure nodes are processed in the order they were discovered, creating breadth-first behavior.

sections.heading: Why BFS?
sections.body:
BFS is the go-to algorithm when you need:

- **Shortest paths** in unweighted graphs
- **Level-order processing** (e.g., level-by-level tree traversal)
- **Minimum steps** to reach a target

Because BFS explores all nodes at distance `k` before any node at distance `k+1`, it **guarantees the shortest path** in unweighted scenarios.

sections.heading: BFS vs DFS
sections.body:
**DFS** (Depth-First Search): Uses a **stack** (or recursion), dives deep into one path before backtracking.

**BFS** (Breadth-First Search): Uses a **queue**, explores neighbors level by level.

Use **BFS** when you need shortest path or level-order. Use **DFS** for exploring all paths, backtracking, or tree depth problems.

sections.heading: Core Template
sections.body:
BFS for trees and graphs follows this pattern:

1. Initialize a **queue** with the starting node(s)
2. Track **visited** nodes (for graphs to avoid cycles)
3. While queue is not empty:
   - Dequeue a node
   - Process it
   - Enqueue all unvisited neighbors

For trees, no visited set is needed (no cycles). For graphs, always use a visited set.

approach: Need shortest path in unweighted graph → BFS
Use a queue (FIFO) to explore neighbors layer by layer
Track visited nodes in graphs to avoid cycles

quiz.q: What data structure does BFS use to ensure nodes are processed level by level?
quiz.explain: BFS uses a **queue** (FIFO) to process nodes in the order they were discovered, ensuring all nodes at level k are visited before any node at level k+1.

quiz.q: Why does BFS guarantee the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
options: It uses recursion to explore all paths
It marks nodes as visited immediately
It explores all nodes at distance k before any at distance k+1
It uses a priority queue to sort paths
quiz.explain: BFS explores nodes **level by level**, so when it first reaches a target node, it has taken the minimum number of steps. All shorter paths would have been explored in earlier levels.
